Why is my business not showing up …
Why is my business not showing up on Google Maps?
First establish whether the profile is missing entirely or simply not appearing for a service search. Those are different problems and need different checks.
By
Updated
29 September 2026
3 min read
The short answer

Search for the exact business name and location, then review the profile dashboard for verification or policy notices. If the profile exists but does not appear for a broader query, investigate relevance and the search context. No single field change guarantees a position.
First, identify the problem

Check the exact business name and address or service area, then try a relevant service query. Record what you searched and where. A private browsing window does not remove every location or contextual influence.
Confirm that you are looking at the correct listing and signed into the account that manages it before changing anything.
1. Review verification and access

Look for a verification request or pending status in the management interface. Follow the requested steps using accurate evidence. Processing and available methods vary, so do not assume a fixed completion date.
2. Review the business description and categories
Check whether the profile accurately represents the main business and genuine services. Correct an inaccurate category, but do not add unrelated categories to chase searches. The
profile guide
explains the wider review.
3. Consider the search location

Local results depend partly on distance and relevance to the query. Seeing a different result from a customer in another area is not automatically evidence that the profile is broken. Keep service coverage accurate rather than inventing locations.
4. Check for a duplicate or old listing

Search for old business names and locations. If there appears to be a duplicate, review the appropriate ownership or duplicate-reporting process before deleting anything. An old listing can have information or history that needs careful handling.
5. Correct genuinely wrong details

Check that the phone number, website and location information identify the right business. Harmless differences such as “Ave.” and “Avenue” are not a reason to assume a ranking penalty. Focus on facts that could send customers to the wrong place.
6. Make the information useful

Review the services, current hours, permitted photos and contact links. A visitor should be able to understand whether the business meets their need. Filling a field is not a guarantee of greater visibility, but inaccurate information can frustrate a real customer.
7. Review feedback and policy notices
Genuine feedback helps people judge the business. Use a neutral
review request process
, not a target count intended to beat a competitor.
If the profile disappeared, check for a suspension or other notification and follow the indicated support process. Do not create a new listing to bypass it.
Work from evidence, then monitor
Record the problem, the correction and its date. Check that the change was accepted before evaluating later visibility. Compare similar queries and periods, with notes about the search location.

How to Ask for Google Reviews Naturally | Adsvio Agency
How to get more Google reviews wit…
How to get more Google reviews without being annoying
Make the request clear, voluntary and easy to act on. The goal is an honest record of customer experience, not a promised rating or a quota.

Invite customers to share honest feedback through a consistent process and provide the review link. Do not screen for satisfaction before deciding who receives the invitation. Google prohibits incentives and selective solicitation of positive reviews.
Make the invitation comfortable
A short request explains what you are asking without putting pressure on the customer. Use a channel they reasonably expect you to use, and let them decide whether to respond.
Do not ask the person to prove they reviewed you or make the service experience depend on their answer.
Four decisions for a repeatable process
Choose an appropriate point after the service.
Assign someone to send the request consistently.
Use a direct review link and test it.
Ask for honest experience in the customer's own words.
Use the same invitation criteria regardless of whether you expect a positive or negative response.
A simple request you can adapt
Get the link or QR option through the available Business Profile controls. Then use a message such as:
Thank you for choosing us. If you would like to share your experience, you can leave an honest Google review here: [your review link]. We appreciate your feedback.
This is a template, not a published customer quote. Replace the placeholder with your real link. A receipt or counter QR code can provide another optional route. Test the destination before using it.
Google provides instructions for sharing a review link in its
review help page
What to avoid

Do not offer discounts or gifts for reviews, buy reviews, request a specific rating or send only satisfied customers to the public review page. Do not provide a script that pretends to be the customer's personal experience.
Review Google's
contribution policy
when designing the process. The request should remain neutral even when the business hopes for positive feedback.
Respond thoughtfully

Thank people for their feedback without revealing personal details. Where there is a concern, acknowledge it and offer an appropriate private contact route. For a practice handling sensitive information, have the responsible person review how public replies are managed.
Do not argue, identify private records or promise a remedy you cannot provide. A short, factual response can be enough.
What to measure

Track whether requests are sent consistently, links work and feedback receives appropriate attention. Review themes that could improve the service. There is no universal review count or response rate that guarantees visibility.

How many reviews do I need?
There is no fixed number that guarantees a position or customer response. Focus on genuine experiences, a consistent invitation process and learning from the feedback.
Should I ask only customers who were happy?
No. Use a neutral process and consistent invitation criteria. Do not screen customers to send only positive experiences to Google.
Can I suggest what the review should say?
Let the customer describe their own experience. Avoid requesting a particular rating or writing a review for them.

Instagram Post Ideas for Small Businesses | Adsvio Agency
What should I post on Instagram fo…
Start with a question someone asks before buying, booking or requesting an estimate. That gives the post a job beyond filling a square on the grid.

Show real work with permission, explain a process, answer a common question or make a clear invitation. Choose examples that fit your service and audience. A manageable schedule and a working contact path matter more than copying a universal posting ratio.
Collect questions before you need a post
Keep a short list of questions from calls, messages and appointments. Remove personal details. Group them around service fit, preparation, price context and what happens next.
A consultant may explain the first session. A realtor may explain an approved listing process. A roofer may describe what information helps arrange an estimate. Use what the business actually does.
Five types with practical examples
Show:
an approved finished project with a clear description.
Explain:
why a step in your process matters.
Introduce:
the person or team responsible for the work.
Answer:
one common pre-purchase question.
Invite:
who the service is for and how to inquire.

For an accountant, preparation for an appointment may be more useful than a generic motivational quote. For a salon, explain a service difference. For a healthcare or legal practice, use approved general information and protect private details.
Turn the ideas into a month

Choose a realistic number of posts and assign each one a purpose. An illustrative twelve-post mix is four work examples, three explanations, two process posts, two answers and one invitation. This is a planning example, not a formula proven to produce leads.
Use the
monthly planning guide
to organize drafting, assets, approvals and publishing. Reduce the volume if quality or accuracy starts slipping.
Replace filler with useful context

Hours and service updates can be useful when customers need them. The problem is a feed that never explains the work. Give a photograph context, describe the actual service and make sure any time-sensitive information is current.
Do not use a stock photograph as proof of your own project or invent a customer story to make a caption more persuasive.
Plan language and format deliberately

Write in a language your intended audience understands and that your team can support in replies. Translate important information carefully when needed. Do not assume alternating languages automatically serves every reader.
A photograph, carousel or short video can each work for a different explanation. Choose the format that makes the point clear and is realistic to produce.
Measure whether the post helps the next step

Look at relevant messages, profile visits and visits to the linked service page alongside reach, saves and shares. Check whether the people inquiring fit the service. Likes alone cannot establish business value.

How often should a small business post?
Choose a schedule you can sustain with useful, accurate material. Start modestly and review the response before increasing volume. There is no universal posting frequency that guarantees inquiries.
Do I have to make Reels?
No. Use video when it helps explain or demonstrate the work. Clear photographs and written explanations can also be useful; review your own audience response.
What if I have no client photos to share?
Use general process explanations, service questions and accurate team introductions. Do not fabricate work examples or disclose private information to fill a content gap.

An honest word about branding

Branding is the part of this industry with the widest gap between what it costs and what it is worth. Agencies will happily sell a small business a $15,000 identity project with a forty-page brandbook, and almost none of that is what the business needed.

What a small business needs is narrow and specific: a mark that works at 32 pixels, two or three colours that hold together, a typeface pairing, and a written rule for what goes where. That is it. It takes a competent designer about a week.
We put branding at $250 to $500 as an add-on because that is roughly what it is worth in the context of a foundation build, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest.
What identity actually has to survive
The very small sizes

Your logo will spend most of its life as a 32-pixel circle: a browser tab, a WhatsApp avatar, a profile picture. Marks that look great on a presentation slide and turn into a smudge at avatar size are the single most common failure, and it happens because they were designed at the wrong size.
One colour, and no colour

It has to work in solid black on a receipt, in white on a dark photograph, embroidered on a shirt, and etched on a window. If it only works in full colour on white, it will fail somewhere visible within a month.
Being used by people who are not designers

You will hand this to a printer, a sign maker, a supplier and whoever posts on your behalf. If the rules are not written down in a form a normal person can follow, the identity drifts within a quarter: three shades of the same blue and two versions of the logo, one of them stretched.
How we work
We start from your business rather than from a moodboard: what you sell, who buys it, what your competitors look like, and what you want someone to feel in the second before they read anything.

Then two or three directions, properly made, not thirty thumbnails to pick from. Each one shown where it will actually live: on a phone, on a sign, on a receipt, as an avatar. You choose a direction and we refine it, rather than you being asked to art-direct.
The goal is not a logo you love in the presentation. It is a logo that still works in three years, at every size, in the hands of people who have never thought about kerning.
